status: DESCRIPTIVE PLANNING -- no hypothesis, nothing fitted, nothing selected, nothing changed. Estimates the operating characteristics of the prospective checkpoint rules before the checkpoint data exists.
why: The live evaluation protocol (research/LIVE_EVALUATION.md, pre-registered 2026-09-21) sets checkpoints at 500, 2,000 and 5,000 prospective shadow hours with verdicts on E012 (skill) at 2,000 and E013 (calibration) at 5,000. It was written without a power analysis, and on 2026-09-22 an 18-hour reading had the model behind the free reference. Both raise the same question: at a given number of live hours, how often would the rules give each answer if the model were exactly as good as it was on validation?
method: Every contiguous N-hour window (step 24h) of the walk-forward out-of-sample validation record that reproduces E013 exactly -- because a live record is a contiguous stretch with its own regime, not a random sample of hours. Inside each window, every statistic is computed from that window alone, as a checkpoint would. A perfectly calibrated control uses outcomes simulated from the model's own probabilities (seed 7): its failure rate is a rule's failure rate from sampling noise alone. The rho interval is a 48h block bootstrap (300 resamples) on weekly-spaced windows at the verdict sizes.
caveats: Assumes the live advantage equals the validation advantage. If it is smaller, every 'hours needed' figure is an UNDER-estimate.
Uses the (worn) validation period -- acceptable for estimating variability, which selects nothing; it would not be acceptable for choosing anything.
Windows overlap, so the shares are not independent draws; they describe how often a checkpoint would land on each answer, not a formal probability with an interval.
results:
(1) THE 18-HOUR WATCH ITEM WAS UNREMARKABLE. With the model exactly as good as on validation, an 18-hour stretch shows it BEHIND the free EWMA rule in 25% of windows. The reading of 2026-09-22 was a one-in-four event; the watch item is closed as explained. The model leads in 92% of 100-hour windows, 97% at 200 and 100% from 500.

(2) THE E012 VERDICT AT 2,000 HOURS IS SOUND: Brier bar 100%, accuracy bar 98%, rho point and interval 100% of windows -- a false-failure rate of about 2% for a model as good as on validation. At 500 hours the same rule would pass only 59-78% part by part, which is why the protocol gives no verdict there.

(3) THE E013 VERDICT AT 5,000 HOURS: the ECE part passes in 100% of windows. The bucket part ('every bucket with >= 100 rows within 0.05') fails a PERFECTLY CALIBRATED forecaster in 8% of 5,000-hour windows from noise alone, and fails the real model in 27%. The difference between 8% and 27% is not noise: the model is calibrated on average but its calibration moves with the market regime (E013 already saw the Platt intercept drift from -0.2 to +0.2 across folds). A live 'not calibrated' verdict at 5,000 hours therefore has roughly a one-in-four prior chance even if the model is exactly as good as it was on validation.

(4) AT THE 500-HOUR FIRST LOOK, ECE will exceed 0.03 in about 90% of cases even for a good model (10% pass; 17% for the perfectly calibrated control): ECE is inflated by sampling noise at that size. Anyone reading the 500-hour numbers must know this in advance.
affected_design: NO RULE IS CHANGED. An 8% noise-failure rate does not justify weakening a pre-registered verdict rule, and changing one because of how it might come out is exactly what pre-registration exists to prevent. What changes is what the protocol says about its own rules: research/LIVE_EVALUATION.md gains a section stating these measured pass rates, so that every checkpoint is read against its known error rates -- a fail at 5,000 hours means 'worse than a one-in-four event for a model as good as on validation', not 'proven miscalibrated', and an ECE above 0.03 at 500 hours means almost nothing. The 2026-09-22 watch item is closed.
